analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil and gas drilling leases along most U.S. coasts, excluding the central and western Gulf of Mexico.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it sat in the House Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee for the entire two-year Congress before expiring in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently barred the Interior Department from selling new oil and gas leases within 50 to 175 miles of the Atlantic, Pacific, Alaska, and eastern Gulf of Mexico coastlines. It grandfathered existing leases but let the Interior Secretary cancel active leases in Florida's coast and the North Aleutian Basin, with the leaseholders paid back under a 1978 law that allows cash or royalty credits. The chairman of the House Resources Committee never scheduled a hearing or vote, and the bill died there when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents and businesses whose livelihoods depend on clean water and intact shorelines: commercial and recreational fishing fleets, tourism operators, and beach communities from Florida to Maine, the Pacific Coast, and Alaska. It also protects the general public's stake in publicly owned offshore lands by keeping them off the drilling market.

how_it_helps.text: It permanently bans new Interior Department oil and gas leases within a protected band—50 to 175 miles depending on the state—off every Atlantic and Pacific coast, including Alaska, converting the annual year-to-year moratorium into a standing prohibition [S2][S3].

It lets the Interior Secretary cancel active leases off Florida's southwest coast and in the North Aleutian Basin, with leaseholders compensated in cash or royalty credits under a 1978 coastal-zone law, ending two of the most contested drilling prospects outright [S3].
It excludes the central and western Gulf of Mexico from the ban, preserving the areas where drilling is established and limiting the bill's economic reach to frontier waters [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding existing leases in the cancellation zones, who would be bought out with cash or royalty credits, and the industry as a whole, which loses access to new acreage off nearly every U.S. coast except the central and western Gulf.

drawbacks.text: The buyout of existing leaseholders—cash from the Treasury or credits carved out of federal royalties—shifts the cost of cancelling private leases onto taxpayers and other royalty recipients [S3].

Removing a large share of the U.S. outer continental shelf from leasing reduces future domestic oil and gas production, which energy-state members have long argued costs jobs and increases reliance on imports.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The environmental and economic protection for coastal communities is broad and permanent, while the costs—buying out a handful of leaseholders and forgoing drilling in frontier waters—are narrower and mostly one-time, though the lost production is real and long-term.

outcome.mechanism: The House Resources Committee referred it to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee and the chairman never brought it up; it died there when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: The bill was referred to the House Committee on Resources on the day it was introduced, January 19, 1999, and never emerged [S5].
Two weeks later, on February 2, 1999, it was sent to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources and the committee requested an executive comment from the Interior Department [S5].
No further action is recorded; the bill died in subcommittee when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas companies and the Interior Department's leasing program gained two more years in which the coastal bans stayed on the books only as annual appropriations riders rather than permanent law, with new lease sales still legally possible wherever no moratorium applied.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil companies and the leasing program

for.name: Rep. Frank LoBiondo
for.role: Sponsor, House Representative from New Jersey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 19, 1999, to make the coastal drilling bans permanent [S1][S5].

against.name: House Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Controlled the committee calendar and subcommittee assignments
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee on February 2, 1999, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: House Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee
against.role: Subcommittee of jurisdiction over offshore leasing
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, a markup, or a vote for the remaining 23 months of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican with no cosponsors listed, and no committee or floor votes were ever taken, so no partisan split is on the record [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Offshore oil and gas drilling companies
industries.note: The bill would have permanently closed most U.S. waters outside the central and western Gulf to new leasing and bought out existing leases off Florida and Alaska. Its interests ran against coastal communities because the cost of drilling risk—spills, fouled fisheries, degraded beaches—falls on the public.
A permanent no-leasing zone would protect fish habitats and water quality that the fishing economy depends on, with no offsetting cost to the industry.

Beach and resort economies from Florida to Maine and along the Pacific Coast would gain permanent protection from the spill risk and industrialization that offshore drilling brings to viewsheds and shorelines.

By carving out the central and western Gulf planning areas, the bill preserved the existing concentration of U.S. offshore drilling there while closing everywhere else, locking in the Gulf's dominant role rather than reducing it.
